source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024/2025) Incoherent Probability Judgments in Large Language Models
finding: Four LLMs gave incoherent probabilities on probabilistic identities (e.g. P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B)-P(A or B) should be 0). The pattern of error matched humans: bias grows with the imbalance of plus and minus terms.
numbers: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, LLaMA-2-70b, LLaMA-2-7b. 24 event pairs (12 weather, 12 politics), 6 judgments per pair. Temperature 0 and 1. Identities with 2 more positive than negative terms (Z7, Z8) showed about twice the deviation of those with 1 more (Z3-Z6).
quote: Respond only with a number corresponding to a probability between 0 and 1.
limits: Single prompt template, one-number answers, 24 pairs only. No chain of thought tested. Does not show the cause, only a fit in spirit to the Bayesian Sampler.
agent_relevance: Single-number probability answers from a model are not coherent by default. A forced sum-to-1 step is a repair, not a formality.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024/2025) Incoherent Probability Judgments in Large Language Models (scale and repeat judgments)
finding: Bigger models were more coherent but none was perfectly so. Repeating the same prompt 5 times at temperature 1 gave an inverted-U between mean and variance of the judgment, as in humans.
numbers: Each prompt resubmitted 5 times at T=1. More parameters meant smaller deviations and less variance in both GPT and LLaMA series. Perfect coherence reached by no model.
limits: Scaling claim rests on two model families and four models. Confounds size with training recipe.
agent_relevance: Averaging repeated samples reduces variance, but shrinks judgments toward 0.5, so averaging alone does not fix coherence.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024/2025) Incoherent Probability Judgments in Large Language Models (Bayesian Sampler bound)
finding: Authors argue the human-like incoherence fits the Bayesian Sampler better than PT+N, but the LLM data do not separate the two models. With zero samples and a symmetric prior the expected identity deviation is 0.5 for Z3-Z6 and 1 for Z7-Z8: the maximum incoherence.
numbers: Bounds 0.5 and 1.0 derived analytically. Authors say the LLM responses 'do not qualitatively differentiate' the two models.
limits: Explanation is a conjecture linked to autoregressive training; no test that discriminates it from PT+N in LLMs.
agent_relevance: Suggests recalibrating by adjusting incoherence, not only by matching frequencies. A reason to prefer coherent outputs over raw ones when stakes are accuracy.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: First direct de Finetti test on LLMs. A linear program finds the largest guaranteed arbitrage profit against model-stated probabilities. No outcome labels are needed. Incoherence is common and varies widely by model.
numbers: 100 stock-days, 15 models, 365,100 elicitations. GPT-OSS-120B baseline mean profit 0.002067 per unit stake (95% CI 0.001471-0.002737); profit of at least 0.1% in 48 of 100 stock-days. Across 15 models profit ranged about 100-fold: 0.002067 to 0.1994 (Mistral Small 3.2).
limits: Domain is stock-return bins; events built by the authors. 'Profit' is a metric, models are not tradable. One main model (GPT-OSS-120B) for the prompt experiments.
agent_relevance: Gives a label-free coherence score our harness could compute over a set of answers before committing.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models (coherence vs accuracy)
finding: Across models, the more coherent were also the more accurate, but coherence differed far more than accuracy.
numbers: Spearman rank correlation of arbitrage profit with Brier score 0.9143 over 15 models. Brier range only 0.1966 to 0.2157. Of 105 model pairs, 101 had profit differences with 95% CI excluding 0, versus 32 for Brier.
limits: Correlation across models, not within a model. Better models may simply be better at both.
agent_relevance: Coherence is a cheaper and more sensitive diagnostic of model quality than accuracy on few items.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models (richer logic, more incoherence)
finding: Incoherence rises when more logical relations link the events: two stocks, joint events, more days.
numbers: Adding the 16 joint-cell events for two stocks raised mean arbitrage profit by 0.00244 (CI 0.001971-0.002961) over the two marginals. Merely putting a second stock in the prompt raised incoherence for the first stock's marginals.
limits: Compared within one model, within-horizon only, because the horizon preamble changes behaviour.
agent_relevance: Sum-to-one is easy for a flat partition; harder with joint and nested events. Keep the guardrail to simple exclusive partitions.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models (elicitation protocol)
finding: Eliciting the full panel of related events in one query drove incoherence nearly to zero (about rounding level). Pairing complements cut it; unrelated pairing raised it.
numbers: Panel elicitation: near zero for GPT-OSS-120B. Complement pairing: significant decrease. Relation-poor pairing: significant increase. Averaging 1 to 5 elicitations lowers profit because it is convex.
limits: One model, one question set. Authors say general users will not query the full panel.
agent_relevance: Strong support for asking all exclusive answers in one call and normalising, not asking each alone.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models (irrelevant context)
finding: Irrelevant text in the prompt raised incoherence, up to ten times. Largest: a stated gut probability of 70% and positive emotion. A statistics hint lowered it; an instruction arm raised it.
numbers: Abstract: irrelevant detail 'can increase incoherence by an order of magnitude'. Significant increases for anxiety, unrelated numeric anchor (phone battery 70%), coffee detail, 10% savings exposure. 'Statistics' arm: significant decrease.
limits: Some arms arguably carry real information. Exact multipliers per arm are in figures not text.
agent_relevance: Keep prompts clean for probability steps; do not paste anchors or opinions into the elicitation call.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Arbitrage and frequentist consistency scores correlate with true Brier score across forecasters. Strength depends on the logical check: conditional checks best, negation and Or weaker.
numbers: Table 2, scraped set, frequentist: Cond 0.87, CondCond 0.71, aggregated 0.85; arbitrage Cond 0.92. NewsAPI set: aggregated 0.49 (arbitrage) and 0.66 (frequentist). Some entries negative: Negation -0.36 (arbitrage, NewsAPI), But -0.24. Forecasters with Brier worse than 0.25 excluded.
limits: Few forecasters (gpt-4o, mini, claude-3.5-sonnet, llama-3.1 sizes, o1-mini, o1-preview, with and without CoT). The authors note part of the link is just that better models are both. MMLU-error baseline correlations 0.38 and 0.55.
agent_relevance: Consistency can be a proxy label for answer quality, but choose the checks: simple negation checks carry little signal.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks (even strong models violate)
finding: o1-mini, a strong reasoning model, still violated checks often.
numbers: Scraped set, arbitrage: Negation avg violation 0.07, 58% of tuples above threshold; Paraphrase 0.07 (56%); Cond 0.11 (60%); frequentist Negation 0.26 (61%). Aggregate frequentist 0.25.
limits: Thresholds defined by the authors (about the (0.5, 0.6) gap).
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode does not remove the need for a hard normalisation rule in code.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks (ArbitrageForecaster: a failed repair)
finding: Patching a base forecaster by arbitraging its answers on related questions improved only the checks it was tuned on. It did not generalise to held-out checks and did not improve Brier score.
numbers: Tested with gpt-4o-mini setups on Negation and Paraphrase; no gain in actual forecasting performance reported. Long-horizon benchmark of 3,000 checks built for 2028.
limits: Small number of setups studied because recursive cost is high.
agent_relevance: Fixing one coherence axis does not make the agent right. G3: pass on something the repair was not fitted to.

source: Fluri, Paleka & Tramer (2023) Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 forecasts violate negation, paraphrase, monotonicity and Bayes-rule checks. Stochastic noise explains little.
numbers: 380 questions, 1220 variants. Strong violations (>0.2): GPT-3.5 negation 52.6%, paraphrase 30.8%, monotonicity 42.0%, Bayes 68.6%; GPT-4 10.9%, 12.5%, 16.0%, 58.8%. Re-asking the same question 4 times: randomness explains under 20% of strong violations.
limits: Temperature 0 and 0.5 only. Forecast truth not scored.
agent_relevance: Larger model helps simple checks but the Bayes-rule check stays near 59% strong violation: do not trust the model to update by Bayes unaided.

source: Fluri, Paleka & Tramer (2023) (prompting for consistency)
finding: Prompting the model to be consistent on negation worked for negation, did not carry over to other checks, and made some worse.
numbers: GPT-4 negation strong violations 10.9% to 2.9% with negation prompting. Paraphrase 12.5% to 17.3% (worse). Bayes 58.8% to 68.6% (worse). GPT-3.5 negation 52.6% to 37.1% but paraphrase 30.8% to 41.3%. Canonical-paraphrase prompt: no clear gain.
limits: Prompt was one system prompt plus one-shot demonstration.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as ArbitrageForecaster: a repair on one axis may harm others. Test repairs on held-out checks.

source: Filbry, Melo & Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Dutch-book scenarios (extensionality, monotonicity, normalization) are violated across separate chats but mostly not within one dialogue.
numbers: 10 ForecastBench scenarios per violation type (30 scenarios) on Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemma-4-31B-it, Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct. Across conversations: violation above 50% of scenarios for almost all model-constraint pairs. Within one dialogue: down to 10% for Gemini and one of 30 scenarios for Gemma.
quote: cross-conversation incoherence reflects the absence of a persistent common representation rather than an inability to apply elementary probability rules
limits: Qualitative yes/no per scenario; no size of violation. Only 30 scenarios and three models.
agent_relevance: Keep the answer partition and its probabilities in one context. Cross-sample voting without a shared frame is where incoherence lives (G4).

source: Filbry, Melo & Gal (2026) (updating)
finding: Without reasoning, LLMs violate Bayes rule when updating. Reasoning plus code execution greatly improves it.
numbers: 20Q: 40 target animals, T=20. ProteinWorld: 5 worlds, 40 runs, T=6. Five models tested without reasoning, three with reasoning, Gemini-2.5-Pro with Python tool. Downstream task loss above 30% for non-reasoning LLMs.
limits: Synthetic tasks; exact KL values in figures only.
agent_relevance: Use code to do normalisation and Bayes arithmetic; keep the model to likelihood judgments.

source: Petridis, Pelechrinis & Obradovic (2026) How Unlikely Is Unlikely?
finding: Verbal probability words from 19 LLMs show sub-additivity on complement pairs, as humans do, but less than humans.
numbers: 11 uncertainty expressions, 19 models. Four antonym pairs tested. LLM pairs closer to exact complementarity than the Mosteller & Youtz human benchmark, most for (improbable, probable) and (unlikely, likely). Models show upward bias on negative words. 'possible' mean: LLM 51 vs human 37.
limits: Words not numbers. Table values not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Do not elicit verbal hedges and convert them. Numbers with a forced sum are more controllable.

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: what works, what fails?
finding: Experts' probabilities over four mutually exclusive exhaustive hypotheses badly overshot 1 (unpacking), while binary complements summed to about 1.
numbers: 50 UK intelligence analysts, 25 per condition. Sum over 4 hypotheses: control M=1.54 [1.33,1.76]; ACH M=1.77 [1.56,1.97]. Binary complement sum: control 0.98 [0.90,1.04]; ACH 0.95 [0.83,1.00].
limits: Fictitious tribe task with truth-serum cue answers; accuracy is against a naive Bayes posterior, not real outcomes. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Exactly our G: forced sum to 1 over exclusive answers. Humans fail on 4-way, not on 2-way. Expect LLMs to need the guardrail most for 3 or more options.

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) (coherentization effect)
finding: Rescaling answers to sum to 1 cut error by 35%. Coherentizing and then averaging 50 analysts cut error by 61%.
numbers: MAE 0.23 [0.21,0.26] raw to 0.15 [0.13,0.18] coherentized, d=0.96, t(49)=6.77. Averaging 50 coherentized: MAE 0.09 (61% cut). Random coherentized chimp 0.21 (analysts better, d=0.64). Simple normalisation gave 0.13 (Baron's analysis).
limits: Accuracy is against a model-derived target. Equal weights; coherence weighting robust over a range of its parameter.
agent_relevance: Normalising is an almost free gain. Normalising beat the more elaborate method here (0.13 vs 0.15).

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) (structured technique ACH hurt coherence)
finding: Training in Analysis of Competing Hypotheses did not help; the untrained control was a little more accurate and more coherent. Coherentizing then removed the gap.
numbers: Raw MAE: control 0.21 [0.17,0.26], ACH 0.26 [0.22,0.29], d=0.43, p=.14. Share of error due to sum violation: ACH .73 vs control .50 (d=0.60, p=.04). After coherentizing the gap is 0.01. Coherentizing effect d=0.69 control, 1.37 ACH.
limits: Medium effect, not significant on accuracy. Single task.
agent_relevance: Procedural scaffolds can raise non-normalised mass. Add code-side normalisation after any structured hypothesis listing.

source: Mellers, Baker, Chen, Mandel & Tetlock (2017) How generalizable is good judgment? A multi-task, multi-benchmark study
finding: Superforecasters beat regular forecasters and undergraduates on coherence tasks too. Earlier work found coherence and accuracy only loosely coupled, except when coherence-based weights were used.
numbers: Survey 2: five Bayesian problems, superforecasters better on each (all p<0.003). Composite good-judgment score versus superforecaster status: biserial r=.46 (Survey 1), .60 (Survey 2); corrected for attenuation .73 and .84. Congruence-bias test t(124.6)=2.19, p=0.030 vs regular forecasters. Pseudodiagnosticity 41%/36%/32%.
limits: Superforecasters who were wrong on Bayes problems were just as wrong as others (1 of 10 error comparisons favoured them). Only two surveys.
agent_relevance: Coherence helps most as a weighting signal. Coherent answers are a marker of skill, not proof of truth.

source: Predd, Osherson, Kulkarni & Poor (2008); Wang et al. (2011); Tsai & Kirlik (2012); Karvetski et al. (2013), as summarised by Mellers et al. (2017)
finding: Weighting forecasters by coherence is reported to beat the simple mean.
numbers: Reported: coherence-based weighting schemes improved aggregate accuracy by more than 30% relative to a simple mean (second-hand figure).
limits: I did not open any of the four original papers; this is a secondary report. Karvetski 2013 page returned 403.
agent_relevance: Weight samples by coherence when aggregating. Needs checking against the originals before use.

source: Zhu, Sanborn & Chater (2020) The Bayesian Sampler
finding: Two experiments favoured the Bayesian Sampler (generic prior mixed with samples) over Probability Theory plus Noise (PT+N) and plain relative frequency, but PT+N still won for a substantial minority.
numbers: Exp 1: 59 participants; best fit Bayesian sampler 67.80% (40/59), PT+N 30.51% (18/59), relative frequency 1.69% (1/59); binomial p=.005; protected exceedance probability .9994. Exp 2: 84 participants; Bayesian sampler 61.90% (52/84), PT+N 38.10%; p=.038; PXP .9911.
quote: The Bayesian sampler trades coherence for increased accuracy
limits: Student samples (age 17-31). Raw-response fits: Bayesian sampler wins only with small sample size N<=17; models not separable up to N<=237; in Exp 2 PT+N wins when N>=24. Without disjunctions, Exp 1 64% vs 34%. Read via a page summariser, not a pdf.
agent_relevance: Incoherence can be a price paid for accuracy when judgments are drawn from samples. Do not assume more coherence always means better.

source: Zhu, Sanborn & Chater (2020) (identity tests in Exp 2: a null)
finding: In Exp 2 most of the probabilistic identities were not different from 0 for weather pairs (cold/rainy, windy/cloudy), unlike Exp 1 with icy/frosty.
numbers: Exp 2 df=83: Z10 t=.240 p=.811; Z11 t=-.946 p=.347; Z12 t=.073; Z13 t=-1.06 (cold, rainy). Exp 1 icy/frosty all four identities p<=.006, Bayes factors up to 17777.
limits: Pair content matters; deviations depend on event probability and correlation. Z1-Z8 values only in figures.
agent_relevance: Incoherence is context-dependent. Model testing needs several event pairs, not one.

source: Vineberg, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Dutch Book Arguments
finding: The converse theorem (Lehman 1955, Kemeny 1955) says coherent betting quotients cannot be Dutch-booked. Main objections: bets can be refused; a sure loss is symmetric with a sure gain (Hajek's 'Czech book'); additivity step shaky; conditionalization and Reflection arguments are diachronic and contested.
numbers: No sample. Named works: Lehman 1955, Kemeny 1955, Lewis 1999 (Dutch strategy), van Fraassen 1984 and 1989, Hajek 2005 and 2008, Christensen 1996 and 2004, Gallow 2019, Pettigrew 2020.
limits: Read via a page summariser; last 5,000 characters of the page not read. Does not cover accuracy dominance in detail.
agent_relevance: Dutch book is a sufficient argument for static normalisation only. It does not license Bayes updating as a rule, so G-rules for revision must rest on other evidence.

source: Gorur, Rago & Toni (2025) Argumentatively Coherent Judgmental Forecasting
finding: A different, argument-based coherence notion: filtering forecasts whose stated reasons contradict their number improved accuracy for LLM forecasters and in human crowds, though most untrained users did not follow the rule.
numbers: GPT-4o accuracy 69% to 80% at breadth 1 after filtering (2923 questions; 1716 kept). 169 festival participants; Labour question: raw mean 60.69 vs market 95, 61.40 and 63.33 after filtering but 29 of 54 and 48 of 54 removed. Crowd study: only 46 of 100 passed attention checks; McNemar chi-square p<.00001 that user coherence disagreed with the authors' notion.
limits: Not probability-axiom coherence. Filtering removes over half of participants, so gains may be selection. Small after-filter samples. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Weak. Reason-answer agreement is a different test from sum-to-one; do not cite it for the Dutch book guardrail.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Representation Consistency for Accurate and Coherent LLM Answer Aggregation
finding: Weights sampled answers by consistency of internal activations; accuracy gains up to 4% over test-time scaling baselines.
numbers: Abstract: four open-source LLMs, four reasoning datasets, up to 4% accuracy improvement.
limits: Only the abstract and first page text were read; 'coherent' here means activation similarity, not probability axioms. Needs open-weight access.
agent_relevance: Not usable by a prompt-only agent; relevant only as a contrast to probability-axiom coherence.

source: Cho & Kweon (2026) Reproducing and Stress-Testing Two Approaches to LLM Reasoning Reliability
finding: Independent reproduction found that probability-aggregation gains over self-consistency vanish outside the original domains.
numbers: Four new domains: paired p>=0.28. BIRD: +2.5 at K=32 (p=0.16), reversing to -0.25 at n=200.
limits: Only the abstract page was read through a summariser. About token-probability aggregation, not Dutch books.
agent_relevance: Caution: probability tricks that look good in the first paper may be noise. Treat single-source gains as [S].
